q: Are "real-world" executive functions typically impaired by normal aging?
o: No - functional assessment is unnecessary during normal aging
Yes - successful aging invariably prevents planning everyday tasks
No - successful aging appears to have little impact on real-world executive function
Yes - a novel executive test alone establishes real-world impairment
explanation:
Successful aging appears to have little impact on real-world executive functions, so actual functional abilities should be assessed alongside test performance (p854).

B. Yes - successful aging invariably prevents planning everyday tasks: The book says successful aging has little impact on these real-world executive functions (p854).
A. No - functional assessment is unnecessary during normal aging: Actual functional abilities should be assessed in addition to neuropsychological tests (p854).
D. Yes - a novel executive test alone establishes real-world impairment: The book distinguishes test performance from actual function and recommends assessing both (p854).

q: On Figure 57-1, what is the prevalence of hypertension among the medical conditions shown affecting cognition in adults 65+?
explanation:
Figure 57-1 lists hypertension in 70% of US adults aged 65 and older among conditions associated with cognitive impairment (p856).

q: What dose of vitamin E showed reduced functional decline in a large trial for mild-to-moderate AD?
explanation:
A large trial in mild-to-moderate AD found reduced functional decline with vitamin E at 2000 IU per day (p860-861).

A. 800 IU/day: This is the minimum vitamin D requirement discussed for bone health (p772); the requested value is 2000 IU per day (p860-861).
C. 60,000 IU/monthly: This is a vitamin D bolus regimen associated with increased falls, not the AD vitamin E trial (p773); the requested value is 2000 IU per day (p860-861).
D. 500,000 IU/year: This is another vitamin D bolus regimen associated with increased falls (p773); the requested value is 2000 IU per day (p860-861).

q: What percentage of MCI patients "revert" to normal cognitive testing over time?
explanation:
As many as 15% to 40% of patients diagnosed with MCI subsequently test in the normal range (p869).

A. Approximately 10% to 15% per year: This is annual progression from MCI to AD, not reversion (p869); the requested value is as many as 15% to 40% (p869).
B. 1% to 2%: This is general-population annual conversion to AD (p869); the requested value is as many as 15% to 40% (p869).
D. 80%: This is MCI progression to AD over 5 to 8 years (p869); the requested value is as many as 15% to 40% (p869).

q: Roughly how many years before clinical symptom onset does underlying AD neuropathology (β-amyloid, neurofibrillary tangles) typically begin?
explanation:
AD neuropathologic processes often begin 20 years or more before clinical dementia symptoms (p862).

D. 5 to 8 years: This is the MCI-to-AD progression interval (p869); the requested value is 20 years or more (p862).
C. 12 months: This is the cognitive/motor onset interval used in the book's DLB discussion (p984); the requested value is 20 years or more (p862).
B. 3 years: This is the ALS survival reporting interval (p991); the requested value is 20 years or more (p862).

explanation:

q: Among PD patients who live 20 years or more with the disease, what proportion is expected to develop PDD (PD dementia)?
explanation:
Upwards of 80% of patients living with PD for at least 20 years are expected to develop PDD (p870).

B. Nearly 50% to 60%: This is bvFTD as a fraction of FTLD diagnoses (p873); the requested value is upwards of 80% (p870).
A. About 15% to 40%: This is the proportion of MCI patients who may revert to normal testing (p869); the requested value is upwards of 80% (p870).
D. About 1% to 2%: This is general-population annual conversion to AD (p869); the requested value is upwards of 80% (p870).

q: What clinical clue (hallucination type + cognitive screen result) is highly suggestive of DLB rather than AD?
o: Visual hallucinations only when MMSE scores are below 20
Auditory rather than visual hallucinations with MMSE scores greater than 20
Visual hallucinations in patients with MMSE scores greater than 20
explanation:
Visual hallucinations in a patient with an MMSE score greater than 20 are highly suggestive of DLB (p871).

B. Marked delayed-recall impairment alone: AD subjects generally have greater delayed-recall impairment than DLB subjects; this is not the specified hallucination/screen clue (p871).
C. Auditory rather than visual hallucinations with MMSE scores greater than 20: The book specifies visual hallucinations for this clue (p871).
A. Visual hallucinations only when MMSE scores are below 20: This reverses the book's greater-than-20 qualifier (p871).
